results.headline: Astronomers pinpoint the origin of a 10 billion-year-old millisecond signal from space
results.evidence: More than 10 billion years ago, something in a distant galaxy gave off an incredibly bright burst of radio waves which lasted just a few milliseconds. In new research published today in Science , our team tracked it back to its origin in a small galaxy filled with many young stars, when the universe was only one-fifth of its current age. Fast radio bursts like this one are a mystery scientists have been trying to unravel for almost 20 years since they were first discovered. Our discovery is the most distant such burst whose host galaxy has yet been identified. We detected the burst, dubbed FRB 20240304B, with the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa, using a system called MeerTRAP which is designed to catch fast-changing transient radio signals from space in real time. The different frequencies of the radio burst arrived at slightly different times. We call this effect “dispersion”, and it happens because the signal has travelled through a lot of electrically charged material in space on its journey to Earth. These calculations confirmed that we were looking at a galaxy 10.6 billion years ago. It contains only about 10 million times the mass of our Sun, which is a tiny fraction of the mass of our own Milky Way galaxy. The host galaxy appears to be a young galaxy still forming many stars, with a very low amount of metal content, and very different from many of the larger galaxies in which most other fast radio bursts have been found. Our discovery has shown for the first time that fast radio bursts were being produced all the way back to around 3 billion years after the Big Bang, during the period when the universe was most actively forming stars and galaxies. results.headline: Marine Biodiversity Drives Ocean Carbon More Than Any Service: Just Seven Datasets
results.evidence: The ocean's carbon-capturing machinery is more dependent on biodiversity than any other ecosystem service science has ever measured — and the scientific evidence for that dependence rests on only seven datasets. That is the most consequential finding of the largest global biodiversity synthesis ever assembled, published Tuesday in Nature Ecology & Evolution by researchers at King's College London and Imperial College London, with collaborators from the Natural History Museum and the Alan Turing Institute. The study's arrival — just 12 days before the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity convenes its first-ever formal review of global biodiversity targets in Yerevan, Armenia — gives policymakers fresh, quantitative grounds for treating marine biodiversity protection not as a conservation goal adjacent to climate action, but as a precondition for it.Redundancy Myth Falls Apart Under Global DataFor decades, a reassuring idea circulated through ecological science and conservation policy alike: ecosystems carry spare capacity. Lose a few species, and others will step in to perform the same functions. This concept of functional redundancy gave policymakers a margin of comfort — a suggestion that extinction need not translate directly into the loss of services humanity depends on.The new synthesis, led by Dr. Emma Moffett, a lecturer in geography at King's College London, dismantles that comfort with the most comprehensive dataset ever assembled for the question. Combining 423 published studies and 222,829 data points across ecosystems — terrestrial, freshwater, marine, and estuarine — more than twice the size of the next largest database of its kind — the team assessed 23 categories of ecosystem services and functions ranging from pollination and water quality to carbon sequestration and biological pest control.What they found challenges the redundancy hypothesis at global scale. Oceanic carbon sequestration produced a Fisher's Z-transformed effect size of 1.48 — by far the largest positive response to biodiversity of any service or function measured. Without this biological pump, scientists estimate atmospheric CO₂ concentrations would be approximately 400 parts per million higher than they are today.The pump's efficiency is not a simple function of the amount of life in the ocean. And the signal they produce — effect size 1.48, the strongest in the study — suggests that biodiversity loss in marine systems would degrade the biological pump in ways that terrestrial carbon loss would not." The ocean result stopped us in our tracks," Moffett said. "Carbon capture at sea responded to biodiversity more strongly than anything else we measured, and yet it's one of the least studied areas we found. If the world is counting on blue carbon to help with climate change, marine life can't be an afterthought." These are precisely the countries that rely most heavily on natural pest control and have the least capacity to substitute it with expensive synthetic inputs. The finding translates a global biodiversity statistic into a concrete food-security risk for the most vulnerable populations.

results.headline: Hittite royal archive with 184 tablets unearthed in central Türkiye
results.evidence: A royal archive unearthed at the ancient Hittite settlement of Samuha, in present-day Sivas in central Türkiye, has shed new light on the Hittite Empire , revealing records of a deadly epidemic, military threats and royal life dating back about 3,400 years. The ancient settlement is known as Samuha in Assyrian and Hittite sources. We validated a number of these new genes in well-studied species, such as in cats, chicken, and arabidopsis, with our partners at Active Site and UCSD, with more extensive wet lab results on previously-unstudied genomes to be released soon. results.headline: First Nuclear Clock Ticks With Thorium-229 in a Crystal at Room Temperature
results.evidence: Physicists have long dreamed of building a clock that keeps time using the heartbeat of an atomic nucleus rather than the electron shell of an atom. That dream has now taken a decisive step toward reality. A team led by researchers at TU Wien, working with partners including the Physikalisch-Technische Bundesanstalt and the Austrian metrology institute BEV, has realized a thorium-229 optical nuclear clock in which a continuous-wave laser is locked directly to a nuclear transition using a rapid feedback loop. The device, described in Nature, operates at room temperature inside a millimetre-sized calcium fluoride crystal and represents the first stand-alone nuclear clock in which the interrogating laser is steered by the nuclei themselves rather than by an external frequency reference. The key to the achievement is one of the strangest energy levels known in nuclear physics. The thorium-229 isotope possesses an exceptionally low-lying isomeric state, first proposed in the 1970s and only recently pinned down at an energy of about 8.3 electronvolts, corresponding to a wavelength of roughly 148 nanometres in the vacuum ultraviolet. Because this energy is so low, the transition can be driven with laser light, something impossible for essentially any other nuclear transition, which typically requires energies thousands of times higher. In 2016, the existence of the isomer was proven through its internal conversion decay channel, and in 2022 researchers achieved the first optical detection of the radiative nuclear decay, refining the energy to 8.338 electronvolts. The final missing ingredient was a continuous-wave laser at 148 nanometres, developed in 2025, which enabled absorption spectroscopy of the nuclear transition and, with it, the possibility of true clock operation. In the experiment, 65 picowatts of vacuum ultraviolet power reached the detector, and the thorium nuclei absorbed about 0.75 percent of the light on the investigated transition, yielding a signal-to-noise ratio of approximately 17 after one second of measurement. By modulating the offset lock frequency between two points on either side of the absorption line, the researchers generate an error signal with a zero crossing at the line centre. Analysing roughly 23 hours of clock data with the Lomb-Scargle method, the team found no oscillation amplitudes above a 5 percent detection threshold established through Monte Carlo simulations, and used the resulting upper limits to constrain dark matter couplings. results.headline: UChicago scientists reveal a Jurassic otter that could chew and swallow like modern mammals
results.evidence: A well-preserved fossil of a 165-million-year-old mammal ancestor from China with hind limbs like a platypus and a broad, flattened tail like a river otter appears to be one of the oldest such creatures adapted for swimming and hunting in the water. Dubbed Megacauda sungei (meaning “big tail”) , the Jurassic mammaliaform also shows the earliest evidence yet of bony structures of the throat that gave this mammal predecessor the ability to feed and swallow like modern mammals—thought to lead to the diversification of mammal species with a wide variety of diets. “This is an incredibly important evolutionary innovation. After mammals chew their food, be it plants or meat, they all swallow it in the same efficient and effortless way,” said Zhe-Xi Luo, the Mila Pierce-Rhoads Professor of Organismal Biology and Anatomy at the University of Chicago and senior author of a new study describing the fossil in Nature . “Once early mammals had this apparatus, each group could develop specialized teeth and diversify into a tremendous range of food resources. They could be carnivores, insectivores, herbivores, omnivores, or anywhere in between.” All modern mammals, including humans, have hyoid bones that link the mouth and throat passage down to the esophagus and the larynx. They are arranged in a U-shaped saddle, suspended by a chain of bony segments to the skull. This helps adult mammals to use throat muscles to swallow chewed food one lump at a time, instead of gulping down huge bites or whole prey like an alligator. In 2019, Luo and his colleagues discovered a tiny docodont from around the same geological age called Microdocodon gracilis , which also had mammal-like hyoid bones. The fossil was discovered in the Inner Mongolia region of China. During the difficult years of the COVID-19 pandemic, study co-author Chang-Fu Zhou from Shandong University of Science and Technology took the specimen to several research labs around the country to have it imaged with CT scanning and X-ray fluorescence photography. The large fossil slab had to be separated into smaller pieces for scanning, but the scans allowed April Neander, a scientific artist and expert on CT imaging at UChicago, to visualize its structures in fine detail. In addition to the intricate hyoid bones and throat structure, the fossil is also preserved with the pelvis, hind limbs, and tail that distinguished it as a powerful swimmer. results.headline: Ancient bird becomes second Australian species to be named from the Cretaceous period | Geology Page
results.evidence: A pair of exceptionally rare Cretaceous bird bones found at separate sites near Richmond, Queensland, reveal a previously unknown species—the second formally named Cretaceous bird from Australia. results.headline: Massive single-nucleus atlas reveals how genetic risk for brain disease
results.evidence: In the largest effort of its kind, researchers have mapped how genetic variants tune gene expression across the human brain one cell at a time. The study, published in Nature Genetics, draws on single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 5.6 million nuclei from the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex of 1,384 postmortem donors, more than a third of whom are of non-European ancestry. By profiling eight major cell classes and 27 finer subclasses, the team built a multi-resolution atlas of expression quantitative trait loci, or eQTLs, the genetic variants that influence how strongly a gene is transcribed. The result is a resource that begins to explain, with unprecedented cellular precision, why genetic risk variants for schizophrenia, Alzheimer's disease and other brain disorders so often act in one cell type and not another. The scale of the dataset matters because statistical power in single-cell genetics is notoriously hard to come by. Most variants identified by genome-wide association studies sit in non-coding regions of the genome, where they are thought to act as regulatory elements that dial gene expression up or down. Bulk tissue studies, which average signals across millions of mixed cells, have linked many of these variants to specific genes, but they cannot resolve which of the brain's dozens of cell types actually carry out the regulation. By aggregating nuclei from each donor into cell-type-specific pseudobulk profiles and fitting linear mixed models that account for population structure, the researchers detected significant eQTLs for 14,258 genes, with 981 genes showing regulatory effects specific to a cell class and 857 specific to a subclass. Much of this variation tracks cell type abundance and average sequencing depth per cell, a reminder that rare but biologically important populations remain underpowered even in a study of this magnitude. Using stratified linkage disequilibrium score regression, the researchers showed that regulatory variants from neurons are enriched for the heritability of neuropsychiatric traits, with schizophrenia showing the broadest signal, followed by bipolar disorder and major depressive disorder. For Alzheimer's, beyond 16 genes in immune cells driven largely by microglia, the team found nine genes in oligodendrocytes, 12 in astrocytes and six in neurons, with microglial genes enriched for amyloid-beta formation and oligodendrocyte genes for complement activation, hinting at an immune-regulatory role for these myelin-producing cells. Because the donor cohort spans the entire postnatal lifespan, from birth to over a century old, the study could also ask whether genetic regulation itself changes over development. Using a supervised pseudotime trajectory anchored to donor age, the researchers tested whether variant effects on expression shift along the trajectory, fitting negative binomial mixed models at the single-nucleus level.
